concept.name: Emission schedule
concept.definition: An emission schedule is the predetermined rule governing the rate and timing of new token issuance over time — the protocol's monetary policy expressed as supply growth per block, epoch or era.
concept.intuition: It is the central-bank timetable baked into code: exactly how many new tokens are printed, when, and for whom, years into the future.
concept.mechanics: Bitcoin emits a block subsidy that halves every 210,000 blocks (50 → 25 → 12.5 → 3.125 BTC...) toward the 21M cap; Ethereum issues ETH per epoch to validators with rates that fall as total stake rises, net of base-fee burns. Application tokens define their own schedules for incentives and treasury releases. Coin Metrics' future-supply metrics formalize projecting supply from the known schedule.
concept.formula: Bitcoin subsidy = 50 / 2^⌊height/210,000⌋ BTC per block; annualized inflation = issuance per year / current supply.
concept.failure_modes: Declining emissions create a long-run security-budget question (fees must eventually fund security alone); for application tokens, front-loaded emissions fund growth but guarantee heavy early dilution and sell pressure.
concept.misconceptions: A fixed emission schedule makes supply predictable, not price — demand shocks still dominate valuation. 'Deflationary' claims require net issuance (emissions − burns) below zero, not just a burn mechanism.
concept.example: After the April 2024 halving, Bitcoin emits 3.125 BTC per ~10-minute block (~450/day, ~0.8% annualized); UNI instead has a 2% perpetual annual inflation beginning in year 4 after its 1B genesis mint.

citations.source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (whitepaper)
